Merchants
mûr'chănts
n. pl. (traders, dealers in wares carried between countries — honoured in Proverbs, indicted in the prophets, and weeping at the fall of Babylon)
From Old French marchant, from Latin mercari, to trade, from merx, merchandise. The Hebrew words rendered merchant are chiefly socher, one who travels about, and rokel, a pedlar or trafficker; and Kena'an, Canaan, is itself used to mean a trafficker.

Biblical Definition

Scripture is not squeamish about merchants. The virtuous woman of Pro 31 is praised in their terms — “She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar” (Pro 31:14) — and she buys a field, plants a vineyard, and makes fine linen and sells it. Trade is a lawful calling and a mark of a functioning society. But Scripture also watches what trade does to a people when it becomes the whole of their life. Tyre is the case study: “the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth” (Isa 23:8), and Ezekiel's lament over her runs for three chapters and ends in the sea. Nehemiah found the sabbath being eroded exactly where one would expect — “the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice” (Neh 13:20), camping at the gates until he threatened to lay hands on them. And the Revelation gives the last word: when Babylon falls, “the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more” (Rev 18:11), and the cargo list that follows ends with an item that indicts the whole trade — “slaves, and souls of men”.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a merchant as one who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who buys and sells goods for profit.

expand to see more

MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods and sells them by wholesale.

In popular usage, any trader, or one who deals in the purchase and sale of goods.

MERCHANDISE, n. The objects of commerce; wares, goods, commodities, whatever is usually bought or sold in trade.

The word is from the French marchand, and ultimately from the Latin mercor, to buy.

In Scripture the merchants of Tyre are called princes, and the merchants of the earth are said to weep at the fall of Babylon.

Key Scripture

Pro 31:14 — "She is like the merchants' ships; she bringeth her food from afar."

Isa 23:8 — "Who hath taken this counsel against Tyre, the crowning city, whose merchants are princes, whose traffickers are the honourable of the earth?"

Neh 13:20 — "So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice."

Rev 18:11 — "And the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her; for no man buyeth their merchandise any more:"

Modern Corruption

Commerce is either sanctified without qualification or condemned as such; Scripture blesses honest trade, forbids the false balance, and reserves its judgment for the traffic that finally deals in souls of men.

expand to see more

Two errors face each other here and both are common in the church. The first baptises commerce entire, treating profit as self-evidently the fruit of virtue and the market as a moral arbiter. Scripture will not: it legislates against the false balance as an abomination (Pro 11:1), forbids interest taken from a poor brother, commands the corners of the field be left unreaped, and cancels debts every seventh year. The second error condemns trade as such and reads Rev 18 as a manifesto against enterprise. That will not stand either — Pro 31 makes a trading woman the model of a godly wife, and the Lord Jesus told parables in which the servant who traded and gained was commended and the one who buried the talent was condemned.

What Scripture actually indicts is a commerce that has become a religion, and it names the point at which the line is crossed. The merchandise of Babylon in Rev 18:12-13 is listed in descending order of luxury — gold, silver, precious stones, silk, scarlet, ivory, marble, cinnamon, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, beasts, sheep, horses, chariots — and the list ends “and slaves, and souls of men.” Human beings appear as the last line item of the inventory, which is precisely how a market that answers to nothing above itself will finally treat them. The traffic in persons is the terminus, and every age finds its own form of it.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Latin merx, merchandise; Hebrew socher (H5503), a traveller, trader; rokel (H7402), a pedlar; Kena'an (H3667), Canaan, also trafficker; Greek emporos (G1713).

expand to see more

Hebrew socher (H5503) — a merchant; from sachar, to go about, travel for trade.

Hebrew rokel (H7402) — a trafficker, pedlar; used repeatedly of Tyre in Eze 27.

Hebrew Kena'an (H3667) — Canaan; the same word means a merchant, and Hos 12:7 puns on it.

Greek emporos (G1713) — a merchant, one on a journey for trade; the word of Rev 18:11 and of Mat 13:45.

Greek emporion (G1712) — a market-house; “make not my Father's house an house of merchandise” (Joh 2:16).

Usage

"“She is like the merchants' ships” — trade as a figure of a good wife's diligence."

"“Whose merchants are princes” — Tyre at the height, and under sentence."

"“The merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her” — the mourning of a lost market."
